doc.title: Ray Shiner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 11, 1998

title: State of jazz today and Hamilton's guests
summary: Jazz in decay under pop and rock; admiration for players who visit Hamilton.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Do you have an opinion about the state of jazz today?

It’s in decay. It’s pop and rock. Not even pop, it’s rock & roll. It’s not even rock & roll it’s — I don’t know what you call it because I don’t listen to it. It’s sickening. It’s noise. Noise is the way I describe it. But of course I’m an old reprobate.
What about fellows like Warren Vache, Scott Hamilton?

Oh they’re great players. No, no, no, those are great players. I love Dixieland. You know you have Dixieland, you have traditional music, you have some of the greatest jazz musicians in the world play here at Hamilton. You know, Warren Vache, you have Kenny Davern, you have, name them, Ralph Sutton.
Yeah. So it’s still happening but it’s an awful small—
You’ve got Joe Wilder here. You had Clark Terry here, which is what brought me here, you had Milt Hinton, which is what brought me here.

You had Frank Foster here. These are all dear friends of mine. You had Bobby Rosengarden. I worked with him when he was with ABC, he was the musical director for Dick Cavett. I had a great life in New York and these guys have never forgotten me and I’ve never forgotten them.
Well that is a good story. Your life’s a good story.
Well I’ve been very fortunate and blessed. I got to meet you, I’m not trying to throw bouquets at you, but you know what I’m talking about, I don’t have to draw a picture for you.
